claims.claim: In 2024, Stonehenge's Altar Stone was traced to Scotland.
claims.note: Published online 14 Aug 2024; title 'A Scottish provenance for the Altar Stone of Stonehenge'; abstract: detrital ages show 'a remarkable similarity to the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland'. True as a dated report of the 2024 result.

claims.claim: Two years on, scientists still can't agree where it came from.
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2026 full text https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jqs.70080 (via Firecrawl); Pirrie 2026 full text https://www.lyellcollection.org/doi/full/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (via Firecrawl); Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/jqs.70080; Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1144/jgs2026-090
claims.note: Clarke 2026 (online 4 Jun 2026) still proposes mainland NE Scotland (Caithness or Inverness-Black Isle) while saying the 'source location within this large basin remains unresolved'. Pirrie 2026 (online 5 Nov 2026, ~2 y 3 m after Clarke 2024) answers Clarke 2026a directly: chrome spinel scarcity 'may indicate that an origin from this part of NE Scotland needs re-evaluating'; Introduction: multi-proxy work 'raises questions over this interpretation'; Conclusions: provenance 'has yet to be determined with confidence'. A live disagreement; 'still' reads as 'even now', which holds.

claims.claim: Hook as heard by a viewer who swipes at second two (A4): the 2024 study placed the stone in Scotland.
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 full text https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07652-1?error=cookies_not_supported (doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1); Pirrie 2026 full text https://www.lyellcollection.org/doi/full/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (via Firecrawl)
claims.note: At ~2 s the viewer has heard at most the first sentence. What they take away (a 2024 study traced it to Scotland) is true. No source says the stone is not from Scotland; Pirrie 2026 says the NE Scotland origin 'needs re-evaluating', not that it is wrong. The year frames it as a report, not settled fact, and the second sentence (and the title) carry the dispute.

claims.claim: The ages of tiny mineral grains inside it
claims.note: Methods: U-Pb, Lu-Hf and trace-element data for zircon, apatite and rutile from two Altar Stone fragments (MS3, 2010K.240); resistive grains 'typically 10-40 um wide'; target grains 'usually <30 um in width'. 'Tiny' is fair.

claims.claim: ...matched sandstone in the northeast.
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 full text https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07652-1?error=cookies_not_supported (doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1); Pirrie 2026 full text https://www.lyellcollection.org/doi/full/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (via Firecrawl)
claims.note: Clarke 2024: 'remarkable similarity to the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland'; KS test 'fails to reject' the null hypothesis; apatite age components from Caithness and Orkney samples 'match those from the Altar Stone'. Pirrie 2026 agrees the similarity holds but notes the same age pattern occurs elsewhere in the Orcadian Basin (Tarbat, northernmost Scotland), still NE Scotland. 'Matched' is about ages only, as spoken.

claims.claim: six tonnes
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 full text https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07652-1?error=cookies_not_supported (doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1); Parker Pearson 2024 full text https://doi.org/10.14324/AI.27.1.13 -> https://journals.uclpress.co.uk/ai/article/id/3293/; Clarke 2026 full text https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jqs.70080 (via Firecrawl)
claims.note: Clarke 2024: 'a 6 tonne shaped block'; 'measuring 4.9 x 1.0 x 0.5 m ... weighing 6 t'. Parker Pearson 2024: 'a 6-tonne monolith'. Clarke 2026: '6000 kg'.

claims.claim: If so, how did six tonnes travel more than seven hundred kilometres?
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 full text https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07652-1?error=cookies_not_supported (doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1); Clarke 2026 full text https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jqs.70080 (via Firecrawl)
claims.note: Clarke 2024 abstract: 'Such a provenance implies that the Altar Stone ... was sourced at least 750 km from its current location'. Clarke 2026: 'some 700 km'. 'More than 700' sits under 'at least 750'; 'If so' keeps the condition the source places on it.

claims.claim: Clarke and colleagues, who traced it
claims.note: First author Anthony J. I. Clarke (ORCID 0000-0002-0304-0484), with Kirkland, Bevins, Pearce, Glorie, Ixer.

claims.claim: ...suggested it went by sea.
claims.note: Abstract: 'The difficulty of long-distance overland transport ... suggests that it was transported by sea.' 'Suggested' matches the source's own verb.

claims.claim: But no late Stone Age boat has been found in Britain
claims.note: 'Although no boats are known from the Late Neolithic in Britain or Europe'; 'The earliest known boats in Britain ... at Ferriby ... Early Bronze Age ... (Ferriby 3) dates to 2030-1780 cal bc'. Holds whether 'late Stone Age' is read as Late Neolithic or the Neolithic as a whole.

claims.claim: ...and a study by Parker Pearson and colleagues doubts one could carry six tonnes.
claims.source_checked: Parker Pearson 2024 full text https://doi.org/10.14324/AI.27.1.13 -> https://journals.uclpress.co.uk/ai/article/id/3293/; Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.14324/AI.27.1.13
claims.note: 'What we know of Early Bronze Age boats ... would suggest that they and their Late Neolithic precursors were unlikely to be sturdy enough to carry a 6-tonne stone in coastal waters'; logboats and curraghs 'would seem even less feasible'. First author Mike Parker Pearson.

claims.claim: Overland, on a sledge, they estimate about eight months of hauling.
claims.note: 'a suitably robust wooden sledge ... sliding on wooden rails'; 'could take perhaps four times today's time of under two months ... needing eight months or so to haul a stone from northern Scotland to Stonehenge'.

claims.claim: A glacier? A 2026 ice model by Clarke and colleagues says ice could have carried it part of the way, at most.
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2026 full text https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jqs.70080 (via Firecrawl); Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/jqs.70080
claims.note: Same first author as Clarke 2024 (same ORCID). Abstract: 'we combine sandstone provenance analysis with ice flow modelling'; 'Glacial transport may have provided an intermediate stage ... but alone cannot account for the final emplacement'. Conclusions: 'Glaciation may therefore have provided, at most, partial transport'; 'Our models do not predict any Late Devensian glacial transport directly to Stonehenge'. Not said, fairly: the paper adds that an older (Anglian) glaciation could have gone beyond the modelled extent but cannot be modelled yet; this does not change its own 'at most' conclusion.

claims.claim: Then, months later, a 2026 study by Pirrie and colleagues
claims.note: Pirrie 2026 published online 5 Nov 2026 (issue Nov 2026), five months after Clarke 2026 (4 Jun 2026). First author Duncan Pirrie.

claims.claim: ...including three of the 2024 team
claims.note: Bevins, Ixer and Pearce are authors of both; no other Clarke 2024 author is on Pirrie 2026.

claims.claim: ...looked closer.
claims.note: Abstract: 'a detailed multi-proxy characterization of the sedimentology, geochemistry, detrital and diagenetic mineralogy of the Altar Stone'; Introduction: 'the most detailed description of the petrography, mineralogy and geochemistry of the Altar Stone to date'.

claims.claim: Many outcrops in that part of Scotland could not have been the source.
claims.note: Abstract: 'many outcrops of the Old Red Sandstone (ORS) in the Orcadian Basin could not have been the source of the Altar Stone'. 'That part of Scotland' = the northeast just named; the Orcadian Basin lies there.

claims.claim: No outcrop examined so far has been shown to match it in every way.
claims.note: Abstract: 'To date, no examined outcrop area of the UK ORS can be shown to have the same suite of lithological and geochemical characteristics'; Conclusions: other ORS areas 'can all so far be excluded when all aspects of the multi-proxy analysis are considered'. The source says 'ORS'; the script's unqualified 'outcrop' still holds, since the Carboniferous candidates Pirrie discusses also differ (zircon spectra; isotopes favour ORS).

claims.claim: Six tonnes, from a spot no one has pinned down
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2026 full text https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jqs.70080 (via Firecrawl); Pirrie 2026 full text https://www.lyellcollection.org/doi/full/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (via Firecrawl)
claims.note: Clarke 2026: 'its source location within this large basin remains unresolved'; Pirrie 2026: 'the exact provenance of the Altar Stone is as yet unknown'. Both sides support it.

claims.claim: ...by a route no one knows.
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 full text https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07652-1?error=cookies_not_supported (doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1); Parker Pearson 2024 full text https://doi.org/10.14324/AI.27.1.13 -> https://journals.uclpress.co.uk/ai/article/id/3293/; Clarke 2026 full text https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jqs.70080 (via Firecrawl)
claims.note: Clarke 2024 suggests sea but names no route; Parker Pearson 2024 thinks 'a land route may have been favoured'; Clarke 2026: 'its mode of transport uncertain'. None claims a demonstrated route.

claims.claim: Sea, sledge or ice: how do you think it got there?
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2026 full text https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jqs.70080 (via Firecrawl); Parker Pearson 2024 full text https://doi.org/10.14324/AI.27.1.13 -> https://journals.uclpress.co.uk/ai/article/id/3293/
claims.note: Offers ice as a third full answer to 'how it got there', on a par with sea and sledge. Clarke 2026, the only cited source for ice, says glacial transport 'alone cannot account for the final emplacement' and that 'substantial anthropogenic transport would have remained necessary' (so ice would come with sea or sledge, not instead of them); Parker Pearson 2024 says glacial theories 'can be rejected'. The earlier line ('part of the way, at most') is right, but this close reverses it for anyone who hears only the end. Change: e.g. 'By sea or by sledge, maybe helped part of the way by ice: how do you think it got there?' or 'Sea or sledge, with or without ice: ...'.

claims.claim: NO FULL MATCH / shown in any outcrop examined / source unknown
claims.source_checked: Pirrie 2026 full text https://www.lyellcollection.org/doi/full/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (via Firecrawl); Clarke 2026 full text https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jqs.70080 (via Firecrawl)
claims.note: 'NO FULL MATCH / shown in any outcrop examined' is confirmed (as claim 18). 'source unknown' drops the qualifier the source uses: Pirrie 2026 abstract says 'the EXACT provenance ... is as yet unknown', and Clarke 2026 still places it in NE Scotland's Orcadian Basin with the location 'within this large basin' unresolved. Both papers agree the rock is most likely ORS of Laurentian (northern) source. Bare 'source unknown' overstates that. Change to 'exact source unknown' (or 'source not pinned down', matching the spoken line).
